procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (inferred, as the High Court heard appeals against convictions)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 29.05.2009 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Appeal Nos. 568, 231 and 250 of 2002.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature at Allahabad heard Criminal Appeals Nos. 568, 231, and 250 of 2002. The High Court set aside the conviction and acquitted the accused from all charges.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State, being aggrieved by the High Court's decision to set aside the conviction and acquit the accused, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court heard the appeal but ultimately dismissed it, finding no serious error in the High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: The credibility of the testimony of an eyewitness (PW-1), who was an advocate and a member of the Nagar Palika, regarding his presence at the scene of the crime at 9:30 a.m. on a working day.

facts: The eyewitness (PW-1) was an advocate with a good practice at the Bar.
PW-1 was also a member of the Nagar Palika and admitted to normally giving hearings to the public in the morning.
The crime occurred at 9:30 a.m. on June 13, 1995, which was a working day.
PW-1 claimed he was at the scene because he was following his deceased brother, who was taking cattle to graze in the jungle.
application: The Supreme Court, agreeing with the High Court, reasoned that a busy advocate and public official would likely be attending to his professional duties at 9:30 a.m. on a working day, not at the scene of the crime.
The Court noted that PW-1's public hearings would have been before court hours, after which he would be expected to go to court.
The Court also found PW-1's conduct to be "unnatural," questioning why an advocate, instead of going to court, would be following his brother to graze cattle.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to reject the eyewitness's testimony, finding it highly improbable that a practicing lawyer and public official would be at the crime scene at 9:30 a.m. on a working day. The court also deemed his stated reason for being there as unnatural and unbelievable.

arguments.issue_text: The credibility of the testimony of an eyewitness (PW-1), who was an advocate and a member of the Nagar Palika, regarding his presence at the scene of the crime at 9:30 a.m. on a working day.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (State) argued that the High Court's acquittal was incorrect and that the trial court's conviction, which was based on the evidence of the eyewitness (PW-1), should be upheld. This implies the State argued that PW-1's testimony was credible and reliable.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (accused) argued that the presence of the eyewitness (PW-1) at the scene of the crime was highly doubtful. They contended that as a lawyer with a good practice and a member of the Nagar Palika who attended to the public in the mornings, it was improbable for him to be at the place of occurrence at 9:30 a.m. on a working day. They also questioned why an advocate would be following his brother to graze cattle instead of going to court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In an appeal against acquittal, an appellate court will not interfere with the judgment if the view taken by the lower court is plausible and does not suffer from any serious and substantial error.
obiter: The absence of bullet holes on the clothes of a deceased who sustained a deep gunshot wound can create doubt about the prosecution's case regarding the time and manner of the incident.

The credibility of an eyewitness's presence at the scene of a crime can be doubted based on their professional and public commitments that would typically place them elsewhere at the time of the incident.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was correct to doubt the presence of the eyewitness (PW-1) at the place of occurrence at 9:30 a.m. on a working day, given that he was an advocate with a good practice and a member of the Nagar Palika who would normally be attending to the public or going to court at that time. The court also found his stated reason for being there—following his brother who was taking cattle for grazing—to be unnatural for a person of his profession.
legal_tests_applied: The standard for appellate interference with a High Court's judgment of acquittal is whether the view taken by the High Court "suffers from any serious and substantial error warranting interference by this Court."
why_appellant_lost: The Court found that the High Court rightly doubted the eyewitness's (PW-1) presence at the scene of the crime, as it was improbable for a lawyer with a good practice and a Nagar Palika member to be there at 9:30 a.m. on a working day.

The Court agreed with the High Court's assessment that the eyewitness's conduct was unnatural, questioning "why an advocate like PW-1 instead of going to the court would follow his deceased brother who was taking the cattle for grazing in the jungle."
The appellant failed to demonstrate that the High Court's decision to acquit the accused suffered from any serious or substantial error that would justify interference.
why_respondent_won: The Court accepted the respondent's argument that the eyewitness's (PW-1) presence was doubtful due to his professional obligations as a practicing advocate and a member of the Nagar Palika who attended to the public in the mornings.
The Court found the eyewitness's explanation for his presence to be unnatural for a person in his position, thereby undermining his credibility.
The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's decision to extend the benefit of the doubt to the accused based on the unreliability of the key eyewitness testimony.
policy_considerations: The judgment reinforces the high threshold for overturning an acquittal, stating that interference is only warranted if the lower court's view suffers from a "serious and substantial error," thereby protecting the finality of an acquittal and upholding the principle of benefit of the doubt for the accused.
